title: American Lawyer's 2026 A-List Ranks Big Law's Top 20 Amid Record Revenue Year
excerpt: The annual ranking, which evaluates firms on financial strength, pro bono work, associate satisfaction, and diversity, arrives as Am Law 100 firms posted 13% collective revenue growth in fiscal 2025.
body:
• The American Lawyer's 2026 A-List ranks the top 20 U.S. law firms across financial performance, pro bono commitment, associate satisfaction, and diversity
  • Am Law 100 firms posted collective revenue growth of 13% in fiscal 2025, with profits per equity partner rising 14%
  • AI and innovation investments are growing faster than any other expense category across Big Law
  • South Asian and Indian-origin lawyers continue to hold prominent leadership positions at several top-ranked firms

The American Lawyer has published its 2026 A-List, its most prestigious annual ranking of the top 20 law firms in the United States. Unlike pure revenue rankings, the A-List evaluates firms on a composite of financial performance, pro bono commitment, associate satisfaction, and racial and gender diversity among partnership ranks — a broader measure of what it calls elite performance.

The ranking arrives against the backdrop of a banner year for Big Law. Am Law 100 firms collectively grew gross revenue by 13% in fiscal 2025, far outpacing the Second Hundred's 6% growth. Profits per equity partner across the top 100 firms rose 14%, with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz leading the profitability charts at $12.15 million per equity partner. Kirkland & Ellis maintained its position as the highest-grossing firm in the country.

What the A-List Measures

The A-List methodology, launched in 2003, aims to identify firms that perform well not just financially but across talent retention and social responsibility. Firms are scored on four pillars: revenue per lawyer, the American Lawyer's pro bono scorecard, associate satisfaction survey results, and diversity metrics covering both racial and gender representation in equity partnerships.

This year's A-List includes firms that have consistently appeared near the top of these individual rankings. O'Melveny & Myers, which topped the Midlevel Associates Survey for the third consecutive year and posted 8.8% revenue growth to $1.2 billion, finished in the top 10. Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom once again ranked among the A-List's top 10, a position it has held repeatedly in recent years.

"We again grew both our top and bottom lines while expanding into areas that enhance our ability to thrive in an ultra-competitive market while fostering a vibrant culture."

— Bradley J. Butwin, Chair, O'Melveny & Myers

A Strong Year With Emerging Pressures

The financial performance underpinning this year's rankings has been driven by robust demand in M&A, private equity, and restructuring practices. Several firms achieved double-digit revenue gains, with Gibson Dunn's profits per equity partner rising to $8.89 million and Paul Hastings reaching $8.33 million.

But rising expenses are beginning to draw attention. A Q2 2026 survey by Law.com found that AI and innovation investments are growing faster than any other expense category. Firms are simultaneously navigating intensified lateral hiring wars and a wave of seismic mergers that have reshaped the competitive landscape.

The pro bono dimension of the A-List remains a differentiator. Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler topped the 2025 Pro Bono Scorecard, followed by Covington & Burling and Jenner & Block. Am Law 200 firms collectively contributed 5.01 million hours of pro bono work last year, with the average attorney at most scorecard firms logging over 100 hours.

The Diaspora Dimension

The diversity metrics that factor into the A-List reflect a broader shift in Big Law's leadership demographics. Indian-origin and South Asian lawyers have become increasingly visible at the partnership level across top-ranked firms, serving as practice group leaders, management committee members, and office heads at Am Law 100 firms.

This trend extends beyond individual appointments. Several firms on the A-List have invested in diversity initiatives that have expanded the pipeline for lawyers from underrepresented backgrounds, including South Asian attorneys who now constitute a growing share of equity partnerships at firms concentrated in New York, Washington, and California.

What's Next

The legal industry's strong financial run may face headwinds as macroeconomic uncertainty, potential regulatory shifts, and the cost of AI integration weigh on margins. The A-List's emphasis on non-financial metrics — talent retention, social commitment, and inclusion — positions it as a barometer of which firms are building sustainable competitive advantages rather than riding a single strong cycle.

The full 2026 Am Law 100 and A-List reports are available on Law.com, with detailed firm-by-firm data on revenue, profits, headcount, and diversity performance.
